ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Psychiatry (eating disorders) Referral — Elisabeth of Austria

code.originalText: New patient visit for weight loss, fatigue, ankle swelling and dizziness: history, examination with orthostatic vital signs, ECG, blood tests, depression and safety screening, a start to nutrition with thiamine, and an eating disorders psychiatry referral

text.paragraph: Weight loss to a BMI of 16.0 with fatigue, ankle swelling, dizziness on standing and a slow pulse in a 56-year-old woman with restrictive eating, frequent self-weighing and hours of daily exercise since early adulthood, and recurrent depression with grief. Please confirm the diagnosis, advise on the level of care and on restarting nutrition safely, and lead a multidisciplinary plan that she can follow while she travels and that protects her privacy. [S]

list.item: Is this anorexia nervosa, another specified feeding or eating disorder, or a medical illness, in a woman of 56 whose restriction began in early adulthood?
Can she be treated as an outpatient, and what findings should lead to admission?
How should nutrition be advanced, given her refeeding risk, and how should she be monitored?
What psychological treatment and team do you recommend, given her travel and her need for privacy?
How should her depression, grief and passive thoughts of death be treated alongside the eating disorder, and when should an antidepressant start?
What should be done about her exercise and her bones?

text.paragraph: Weight 47.4 kg at 172 cm (BMI 16.0), about 6 kg lost over six months; for decades she has kept her weight below a fixed 50 kg, eaten single-food meals, laced tightly, weighed herself up to three times a day, walked four to six hours a day and done gymnastics each morning. Fatigue, cold intolerance, 1+ pitting edema of both ankles, and dizziness on standing. No vomiting, laxatives, diuretics or diet pills. Last menstrual period in her late forties. Seated blood pressure 96/62, pulse 52, temperature 36.0 C; lying 98/64 with pulse 50, standing after two minutes 86/58 with pulse 66. ECG: sinus bradycardia 52, QTc 438 ms, low voltage. Hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, MCV 93 fL, white cells 3.4 x10^3/uL, platelets 168 x10^3/uL, sodium 136 and potassium 3.6 mmol/L, urea nitrogen 21 mg/dL, creatinine 0.56 mg/dL, glucose 68 mg/dL, magnesium 1.8 mg/dL, phosphate 3.0 mg/dL, albumin 4.1 g/dL, ALT 52 U/L, TSH 2.2 mIU/L, CRP 1.0 mg/L, tissue transglutaminase IgA negative, ferritin 64 ng/mL, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 22 ng/mL. PHQ-9 16 with passive thoughts of death and no intent or plan; a safety plan is in place. Her son died five years ago and she has worn mourning since. Started today: thiamine 100 mg daily, vitamin D, and a meal plan of about 1,600 kcal a day. She travels for weeks at a time and is a public figure who fears exposure [S]

list.item: She is frightened of gaining weight and of losing control of her body, but is exhausted and dizzy and knows she cannot go on like this. [S]
She does not want anyone, including clinic staff, to discuss her weight or her visits, and fears her illness becoming public. [S]
She cannot stay in one place for long and will be travelling for weeks at a time. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Elisabeth Amalie Eugenie, Duchess in Bavaria, called Sisi, was born on December 24, 1837, in Munich, the daughter of Duke Max in Bavaria and Duchess Ludovika. [D]
She married her cousin, Emperor Franz Joseph I, on April 24, 1854, in the Augustinerkirche in Vienna, and became Empress of Austria and, later, Queen of Hungary. She had four children. [D]

From about 1859 she was reported to suffer from a mysterious illness, with cough, poor nutrition, anemia and exhaustion; she spent the winter of 1860 to 1861 on Madeira and, after a relapse, four months on Corfu, and recovered quickly whenever she travelled. [D]
At 1.72 m she was unusually tall for a woman of her time, with an extremely slender figure. [D]

Through her life she followed many diets; for periods each meal was a single food, such as egg, a milk product, orange or broth, and her 'magic weight' was fifty kilos. In her last years she weighed herself up to three times a day, and in 1894 she weighed as little as 43.5 kg, a body mass index of about 14.7 at her height. [D]
Her waist measured only about 50 cm at its smallest, in tightly laced corsets and dresses sewn around it. [D]

She hiked for hours every day and had exercise rooms installed in her apartments; in the Vienna Hofburg the wall bars, high bar and rings are preserved, and she had a large gymnasium with heavy apparatus. She was one of the best horsewomen in Europe, but gave up riding at the beginning of the 1880s because of health problems. [D]

A psychiatrist's biographical essay writes that in her last years she was increasingly troubled by her undernutrition, with fluid accumulation in the body and severe bodily pains, and that she was diagnosed with chlorosis. [D]
Eating-disorder researchers write that she sometimes suffered from edema as a consequence of severe starvation. [R]

A Swiss newspaper reported in 2024 that letters kept by her spa physician at Bad Kissingen, found in the city archive, describe complaints including rheumatic attacks, sciatica, joint pain and hunger edema at the ankles. [D]

Psychiatrists and eating-disorder researchers have argued that she met the criteria for anorexia nervosa: one essay states that 'without doubt' she qualified, a German study describes fasting rituals, gymnastics, hours of riding, forced marches and a considerable fear of weight gain, and Hungarian researchers describe many features of anorexia nervosa and suggest it was closely related to depression. [R]

On January 30, 1889, her son, Crown Prince Rudolf, born in 1858, was found dead with a young woman at the Mayerling hunting lodge; historians regard as certain only that he killed her and then himself. [D]

It is said that her son's death prompted her to wear only mourning from then on. She suffered from ever-deepening depressions, which in her last years are thought to have developed into a kind of death-wish. [D]

After her son's death she sought to master her inner unrest with extended travels and a retreat to Corfu, where she had the Achilleion, a palatial villa, built; she lost interest in it once it was finished and left the island six years after its completion. She often travelled incognito. [D]

list.item: Weight loss to a body mass index of 16.0 (47.4 kg at 172 cm), about 6 kg over six months, with fatigue, swelling of both ankles, dizziness on standing, slow pulse and cold intolerance; cause not established at intake; a restrictive eating disorder suspected, with thyroid disease, celiac disease, diabetes, malignancy and adrenal insufficiency to be excluded; eating disorders psychiatry consultation requested: active, confirmed [S]
Major depressive disorder, recurrent, moderate, with persistent grief for her son, who died five years ago; passive thoughts of death without intent or plan at intake: active, confirmed [S]

Medical assessment and stabilization: orthostatic vital signs and temperature, ECG, blood count, electrolytes with phosphate and magnesium, glucose, kidney and liver tests, albumin, TSH, CRP, ferritin and vitamin D; admission criteria explained; electrolytes, phosphate and magnesium to be rechecked three to four days after the meal plan starts, then weekly for the first weeks. Guideline: The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Eating Disorders, Fourth Edition (2023); Medical Management of Restrictive Eating Disorders in Adolescents and Young Adults (position paper) (2022); Eating Disorders: A Guide to Medical Care (AED Medical Care Standards Guide), 4th edition (2021) [S]

Refeeding risk: thiamine 100 mg daily before and during the first two weeks, and a starting meal plan of about 1,600 kcal a day in three meals and two snacks, increased by about 200 to 300 kcal every few days. Guideline: Medical Management of Restrictive Eating Disorders in Adolescents and Young Adults (position paper) (2022); ASPEN Consensus Recommendations for Refeeding Syndrome (2020) [S]

Collaborative safety plan with warning signs, coping steps, people to contact including her travelling companion, the clinic number, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and local emergency numbers abroad; medicines dispensed in small supplies and kept by her companion. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024) [S]

Privacy: the chart is flagged as restricted, access is audited, she is booked under a scheduling alias at the first or last appointment of the day, and weights are discussed only in the consulting room. Guideline: The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Eating Disorders, Fourth Edition (2023) [S]
